name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q01 - Terms not technically correct for floral whorl

questiontext.text:
Among the terms listed below, those that of are not technically correct names for a floral whorl are:

i. Androecium
ii. Carpel
iii. Corolla
iv. Sepal

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical angiosperm flower consists of four floral whorls arranged on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium. Each whorl is composed of individual floral appendages or units.

Step 2: Evaluation
Androecium is the whorl of stamens, and corolla is the whorl of petals; both are technically correct names for floral whorls. In contrast, a sepal is an individual unit of the calyx whorl, and a carpel is an individual unit of the gynoecium whorl, rather than names of floral whorls themselves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, carpel and sepal are not technically correct names for a floral whorl.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q02 - Analogy between embryo sac and anther

questiontext.text: Embryo sac is to ovule as ______ is to an anther.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In flowering plants, the ovule represents the megasporangium, which houses the female gametophyte (embryo sac). Similarly, the anther contains microsporangia, which produce and house the male gametophytes.

Step 2: Evaluation
The pollen grain represents the male gametophyte developed inside the microsporangium of an anther, making it the direct counterpart to the embryo sac inside an ovule. Stamen, filament, and androecium are sporophytic floral structures rather than the male gametophyte.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, embryo sac is to ovule as pollen grain is to an anther.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q03 - Arrangement of floral whorls on thalamus

questiontext.text: In a typical complete, bisexual and hypogynous flower the arrangement of floral whorls on the thalamus from the outermost to the innermost is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A complete, bisexual, hypogynous flower bears all four floral whorls on the thalamus, with the gynoecium occupying the highest central position.

Step 2: Evaluation
Moving from the outermost periphery to the innermost center on the thalamus, the floral whorls are arranged in the sequence: calyx (outermost whorl of sepals), followed by corolla (whorl of petals), then androecium (male reproductive whorl of stamens), and finally gynoecium (innermost female reproductive whorl of carpels).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct outermost-to-innermost sequence is calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q04 - Dicot plant never produces fruits and seeds

questiontext.text: A dicotyledonous plant bears flowers but never produces fruits and seeds. The most probable cause for the above situation is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In flowering plants, fruits develop from the ovary and seeds develop from the ovules, both of which are parts of the pistil (gynoecium) present in pistillate or bisexual flowers.

Step 2: Evaluation
A monoecious plant bears both male and female flowers on the same individual, and a plant bearing pistillate flowers can receive pollen from male plants to form fruits and seeds. However, if a plant is dioecious and bears only staminate (male) flowers, it completely lacks pistils, ovaries, and ovules, so it can never produce fruits and seeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the most probable cause is that the plant is dioecious and bears only staminate flowers.

answer.text: Plant is dioecious and bears only pistillate flowers
Plant is dioecious and bears both pistillate and staminate flowers
Plant is dioecious and bears only staminate flowers.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q05 - Outermost and innermost wall layers of microsporangium

questiontext.text: The outermost and innermost wall layers of microsporangium in an anther are respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical microsporangium in an angiosperm anther is surrounded by four distinct wall layers that protect the sporogenous tissue and aid in dehiscence and nourishment.

Step 2: Evaluation
From the outside to the inside, the four wall layers are the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, and tapetum. The epidermis forms the outermost protective layer, while the tapetum forms the innermost nutritive layer surrounding the sporogenous tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the outermost and innermost wall layers of a microsporangium are epidermis and tapetum, respectively.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q06 - Site of meiosis during microsporogenesis

questiontext.text: During microsporogenesis, meiosis occurs in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Microsporogenesis is the process of formation of haploid microspores from a diploid microspore mother cell (pollen mother cell) through meiotic division.

Step 2: Evaluation
As the anther develops, cells of the sporogenous tissue differentiate into diploid microspore mother cells, each of which undergoes meiosis to produce a cluster of four haploid cells called a microspore tetrad. Endothecium is a sterile wall layer, whereas microspore tetrads and pollen grains are already haploid products formed after meiosis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, during microsporogenesis, meiosis occurs in microspore mother cells.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q07 - Terms associated with the gynoecium

questiontext.text: From among the sets of terms given below, identify those that are associated with the gynoecium.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The gynoecium is the female reproductive part of the flower and consists of one or more pistils (carpels), each comprising a stigma, style, and ovary containing ovules attached to the placenta.

Step 2: Evaluation
Stigma, ovule, embryo sac, and placenta are all structures belonging to the gynoecium. In contrast, thalamus is the swollen floral axis supporting all whorls, tapetum is a wall layer of the anther, and stamen is the male reproductive organ.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the set of terms associated exclusively with the gynoecium is stigma, ovule, embryo sac, placenta.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q08 - Sequence of parts in an ovule

questiontext.text: Starting from the innermost part, the correct sequence of parts in an ovule are,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An angiosperm ovule (megasporangium) consists of concentric tissues and structures enclosing the female gametophyte and the egg cell.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the innermost region lies the egg cell as part of the egg apparatus inside the embryo sac (female gametophyte). The embryo sac is embedded within the central mass of parenchymatous cells called the nucellus, which in turn is surrounded by protective envelopes known as integuments.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Starting from the innermost part, the correct sequence is egg, embryo sac, nucellus, integument.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q09 - Features of typical female gametophyte

questiontext.text:
From the statements given below choose the option that are true for a typical female gametophyte of a flowering plant:

i. It is 8-nucleate and 7-celled at maturity
ii. It is free-nuclear during the development
iii. It is situated inside the integument but outside the nucellus
iv. It has an egg apparatus situated at the chalazal end

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In most angiosperms, a single functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac) via monosporic development involving three rounds of free-nuclear mitotic divisions followed by cell wall formation.

Step 2: Evaluation
At maturity, a typical embryo sac is 8-nucleate and 7-celled (three cells in the egg apparatus, three antipodals, and one central cell with two polar nuclei), and its early mitotic nuclear divisions are free-nuclear without immediate cytokinesis. However, it is located inside the nucellus (not outside it), and its egg apparatus is situated at the micropylar end (while antipodals are at the chalazal end).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, only the statements that it is 8-nucleate and 7-celled at maturity and that it is free-nuclear during development are true.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q10 - Condition for autogamy in chasmogamous flower

questiontext.text: Autogamy can occur in a chasmogamous flower if:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Autogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower. In open (chasmogamous) flowers, complete autogamy is relatively rare and requires specific floral adaptations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Autogamy in a chasmogamous flower requires synchrony in pollen release and stigma receptivity, meaning both pollen and ovules must mature simultaneously. If either pollen or ovules mature earlier (dichogamy), self-pollination within the same flower is prevented.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, autogamy can occur in a chasmogamous flower if both pollen and ovules mature simultaneously.

answer.text: Both anther and stigma are of equal lengths.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q11 - Correct statement on cleistogamous and chasmogamous flowers

questiontext.text: Choose the correct statement from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cleistogamous flowers are closed flowers that do not open at all, whereas chasmogamous flowers are open flowers with exposed anthers and stigmas.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because cleistogamous flowers remain closed, there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma, so they are invariably autogamous (always exhibit autogamy) and cannot exhibit geitonogamy. Chasmogamous flowers can exhibit autogamy, geitonogamy, or xenogamy depending on floral biology and pollinators.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the correct statement is that cleistogamous flowers always exhibit autogamy.

answer.text: Cleistogamous flowers exhibit both autogamy and geitonogamy

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q12 - Pollination by wind adaptations

questiontext.text: A particular species of plant produces light, non-sticky pollen in large numbers and its stigmas are long and feathery. These modifications facilitate pollination by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abiotic and biotic pollinating agents require distinct floral and pollen adaptations to ensure successful pollen transfer.

Step 2: Evaluation
Wind-pollinated (anemophilous) plants produce enormous amounts of light, dry, non-sticky pollen grains so they can be easily carried by air currents. Their stigmas are often large, long, and feathery to effectively trap airborne pollen grains.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, these modifications facilitate pollination by wind.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q13 - Condition preventing both autogamy and geitonogamy

questiontext.text: From among the situations given below, choose the one that prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Autogamy is self-pollination within the same flower, while geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen between different flowers on the same plant.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a monoecious plant with unisexual flowers, autogamy is prevented, but geitonogamy can still occur between male and female flowers on the same plant. In plants with bisexual flowers, both autogamy and geitonogamy are possible. However, in a dioecious plant bearing only male or female flowers on separate individuals, neither autogamy nor geitonogamy can occur, enforcing xenogamy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, a dioecious plant bearing only male or female flowers prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

answer.text: Dioecious plant bearing only male or female flowers

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q14 - Ploidy of structures in fertilised embryo sac

questiontext.text: In a fertilised embryo sac, the haploid, diploid and triploid structures are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During double fertilisation in angiosperms, one haploid male gamete fuses with the haploid egg cell (syngamy), and the other haploid male gamete fuses with the two haploid polar nuclei (triple fusion).

Step 2: Evaluation
The synergids and antipodal cells remain haploid (\(n\)). Syngamy produces a diploid (\(2n\)) zygote, whereas triple fusion produces a triploid (\(3n\)) primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, in a fertilised embryo sac, the haploid, diploid and triploid structures are synergid, zygote and primary endosperm nucleus, respectively.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q15 - Cells that degenerate after fertilisation

questiontext.text: In an embryo sac, the cells that degenerate after fertilisation are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After double fertilisation, the embryo sac undergoes post-fertilisation changes in which the zygote develops into the embryo and the primary endosperm cell develops into the endosperm.

Step 2: Evaluation
Once fertilisation is completed, the synergids (which guided the pollen tube) and the antipodal cells no longer have a functional role and degenerate, whereas the zygote (formed from the egg) and the primary endosperm cell persist to form the embryo and endosperm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the cells that degenerate after fertilisation are synergids and antipodals.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q16 - Artificial hybridization in dioecious plants

questiontext.text: While planning for an artificial hybridization programme involving dioecious plants, which of the following steps would not be relevant:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Artificial hybridisation involves controlled pollination using desired pollen while preventing contamination of the stigma by unwanted pollen.

Step 2: Evaluation
Emasculation is the removal of anthers from a bisexual flower before anther dehiscence to prevent self-pollination. Since dioecious plants bear unisexual male and female flowers on separate plants, the female flowers already lack anthers, making emasculation unnecessary. However, bagging of female flowers, collection of pollen, and dusting of pollen on the stigma remain essential steps.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, emasculation would not be relevant in an artificial hybridisation programme involving dioecious plants.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q17 - Homologous structures in dicot and grass embryos

questiontext.text: In the embryos of a typical dicot and a grass, true homologous structures are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Homologous structures share a common embryonic origin and fundamental structural identity, even if they are modified in form across different groups.

Step 2: Evaluation
A typical dicotyledonous embryo possesses two cotyledons, whereas a monocotyledonous grass embryo possesses a single large, shield-shaped cotyledon called the scutellum situated towards one side of the embryonal axis. Coleorhiza and coleoptile are protective sheaths unique to monocot embryos.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, cotyledons and scutellum are true homologous structures in the embryos of a typical dicot and a grass.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q18 - Embryo formation without fertilisation

questiontext.text: The phenomenon observed in some plants wherein parts of the sexual apparatus is used for forming embryos without fertilisation is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain flowering plants have evolved special mechanisms to produce seeds without undergoing fertilisation, mimicking sexual reproduction.

Step 2: Evaluation
Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction, in which embryos (and seeds) are formed from parts of the sexual apparatus without fertilisation. In contrast, parthenocarpy refers to fruit development without fertilisation, producing seedless fruits.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, this phenomenon is called apomixis.

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q19 - Ploidy of embryo sac without meiosis

questiontext.text: In a flower, if the megaspore mother cell forms megaspores without undergoing meiosis and if one of the megaspores develops into an embryo sac, its nuclei would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The megaspore mother cell (MMC) is a diploid (\(2n\)) cell. Normally, it undergoes reductional division (meiosis) to form haploid (\(n\)) megaspores.

Step 2: Evaluation
If the diploid megaspore mother cell forms megaspores without undergoing meiosis, the resulting megaspores retain the diploid (\(2n\)) chromosome number. Subsequent mitotic divisions of a diploid megaspore to form an embryo sac preserve the diploid ploidy in all resulting nuclei.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, all nuclei in such an embryo sac would be diploid.

answer.text: A few haploid and a few diploid

name.text: BIOLOGY_CH02_MCQ_Q20 - Ovary develops into fruit without fertilisation

questiontext.text: The phenomenon wherein, the ovary develops into a fruit without fertilisation is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In most flowering plants, fruit development from the ovary is triggered after fertilisation, but in certain species or under hormonal influence, fruits can form without fertilisation.

Step 2: Evaluation
The development of an ovary into a fruit without fertilisation is known as parthenocarpy, and such fruits (like banana) are typically seedless. Apomixis, by contrast, is the formation of seeds and embryos without fertilisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the phenomenon wherein the ovary develops into a fruit without fertilisation is called parthenocarpy.
